The Sphinx. A winged creature with a human head, typically depicted as female, and the body of a lion, who posed a deadly riddle to travelers at the gates of Thebes. She had the face and upper body of a beautiful woman, the wings of an eagle or bat, and the powerful haunches and tail of a lion. Her famous riddle was this: What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening? The answer was humanity, in its stages of life.

She had been sent by the gods as a plague upon Thebes, devouring anyone who failed to answer her riddle correctly. Oedipus, despite his youth and lowly status, approached her fearlessly and solved the riddle with intelligence rather than strength. In rage and humiliation at being bested, the Sphinx threw herself from her perch, dying on the rocks below. Some accounts suggest she had been immortal and that her defeat defied prophecy, breaking a divine curse over the city. Her parentage varied in different versions—some claimed she was the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, others that she had different divine parents. Her intelligence and use of cunning over brute force distinguished her from many other classical monsters.
